title: [Tech Thoughts] Considering AI to help you think through problems? Same here.
summary: Would inviting a little AI into my life help with brain fog at work? It might be able to help, but it'll take time to know how useful it'll be in the long run.

blocks.text: Would inviting a little AI into my life help with brain fog at work? It might be able to help, but it'll take time to know how useful it'll be in the long run.

items: The author reflects on their ongoing struggles with brain fog and cognitive difficulties following a COVID-19 illness, impacting their ability to write and plan effectively.
Despite initial resistance, the author considers integrating AI tools into their workflow as a potential solution to help manage their cognitive challenges and improve productivity.
Encouraged by his wife, the author plans to explore how AI can assist in organizing thoughts and tasks, recognizing it as a tool that could alleviate some of his struggles.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
It’s been a strange few years since COVID-19 came about.

I fell ill from it a few years back, and without noticing it, it slowly dawned on me that I’d been struggling with my thoughts. In the years following getting sick with COVID-19 and recovering from it, it felt as if I had never completely recovered.
I felt like I was suffering from brain fog and had trouble imagining what my days would look like or how to plan and organize my writing.

For a while, reading would help. I’d read up on topics I wanted to discuss for this column, for example, and I’d be able to react to the information. There was, however, a decided difficulty in being proactive.

It’s as if I wanted to go for a walk in a field and was suddenly stopped by vision-obscuring trees everywhere I looked. I had information and things I wanted to do (and deadlines, to boot), but I had trouble planning properly because I couldn’t connect my thoughts into plans, and put plans into action.

There’s no definitive way to test for what caused my brain fog — the American Brain Foundation says it could be a symptom of being sick from COVID-19, chronic fatigue syndrome, insomnia, or even lyme disease. Adding to that, there’s no official diagnosis for this feeling or sensation of being slower than I used to be, but it has threatened one of the things I hold dear to me: my ability to write stuff the way I want to.
My wife, whom I recently shared these feelings of anxiety with, told me something that felt both logical and like a betrayal of the things I write about here when it comes to artificial intelligence.

She advised me to get used to the idea of adding even just a little AI to my life. I tried to imagine it in much the way I would use eyeglasses, or to put it back to the analogy of my suddenly-appearing mental forest, perhaps I could use it like a chainsaw that wouldn’t cut down everything in my path, but would help with some of the trees in front of me.
Maybe using AI could help me see the outlines in my mind a little better.
It started with little things, like audio transcription for work quotes, which worked well enough.
Like any other tool, it felt like I was being forced to adjust to or relearn something I could do myself. But I kept trying anyway.

Quietly, I’d rely on AI search results to help me sift through information just a little faster, or use the work-based AI-powered summarizer on our content on Rappler for a three-sentence overview. I’d check the outputs for accuracy or truthfulness, fix any issues and, in the case of AI searches, make sure to cite the appropriate sources.
These were helpful, but it left me scared too. Could it help me be more proactive? Can it plot out points of action so I could have more information as to what story leads might be pursuable?
Honestly, I wasn’t sure and I didn’t know, and that’s one other point of fear.

I’d been focused on the potential problems AI can bring — from the environmental to the economic and moral implications of AI use — that it didn’t dawn on me that with some work, it could be just a simple tool for helpful solutions for people having trouble with cognition or planning.
My wife, who put this idea in my head, knows well-enough about using AI to help with her unfathomable workload.
Tonight seems like a good time to ask about what tools she uses to get her job done, and maybe learn how to better use AI to shore up my now-glaring weaknesses. – Rappler.com
